title: Pork bacon vs turkey bacon: which has less fat, sodium, and calories?
excerpt: Turkey bacon is often lower in fat and calories, but it may contain as much or more sodium than pork bacon. Compare equal portions before choosing.
seo_title: Pork bacon vs turkey bacon: fat, sodium, calories
seo_description: Compare pork and turkey bacon for calories, total fat and sodium. Turkey is often leaner, but the lower-sodium choice depends on the specific label.
image_query: pork bacon and turkey bacon cooked side by side
image_prompt: Realistic overhead photo of cooked pork bacon and turkey bacon in equal portions on a simple plate, natural light, no text
body:
Turkey bacon is usually lower in fat and calories than traditional pork bacon, but it is not automatically lower in sodium. USDA reference foods illustrate the point: cooked pork bacon can be around 468 calories and 35.1 grams of fat per 100 grams, while a cooked turkey-bacon reference is about 368 calories and 25.9 grams of fat. In those same example entries, sodium is roughly 1,680 milligrams for pork bacon versus about 2,020 milligrams for turkey bacon.

The practical lesson is to compare labels, not animal names. “Turkey” tells you what the product is based on; it does not guarantee a low-sodium or minimally processed food.

Turkey bacon usually wins on fat and calories

Traditional bacon is made from a naturally fatty cut of pork. Cooking renders out some of that fat, but the finished strips remain calorie dense. Turkey bacon is generally made from seasoned, formed or chopped turkey with added fat and other ingredients. Manufacturers can formulate it with less total fat than conventional pork bacon, which is why the calorie difference is often noticeable.

That advantage depends on portion size. One brand may define a serving as one slice and another as two or three. Slice thickness also varies. If the goal is a meaningful comparison, line up the gram weight rather than comparing the numbers printed beside unequal serving sizes.

Cooking method can shift the amount of fat that ends up on the plate as well. Pan-frying, baking and blotting remove different amounts of rendered fat. The package nutrition information remains the best starting point for the specific product you use.

Pork bacon vs turkey bacon in a reference comparison

Per 100 g cooked, example USDA entriesPork baconTurkey bacon
Calories≈468 kcal≈368 kcal
Total fat≈35.1 g≈25.9 g
Sodium≈1,680 mg≈2,020 mg

These numbers are examples from particular reference foods, not averages that every brand must match. They show why turkey bacon cannot be assumed to be lower in every nutrient. A leaner formulation can still rely heavily on salt for flavor, preservation and texture, and brands use different recipes.

Protein is present in both products, but bacon is not the only way to add protein to breakfast. Eggs, plain Greek yogurt, beans, fish or unprocessed poultry can provide protein with a very different sodium and fat profile. That wider context matters more than trying to make bacon function as a “health food.”

Sodium can reverse the apparent winner

High sodium intake can raise blood pressure in salt-sensitive people and is a major reason nutrition guidance emphasizes limiting excess salt. Bacon is concentrated and salty, so checking milligrams of sodium per realistic serving is worthwhile. If you routinely eat four slices but the label serving is two, the number on the panel needs to be doubled.

Both pork bacon and turkey bacon are processed meats when they are cured, salted, smoked or otherwise processed for preservation or flavor. Substituting turkey does not erase that category. Frequency is therefore another useful lever: eating a small serving occasionally is different from making processed meat the default protein every morning.

Claims such as “uncured” or “no nitrites added” answer a different question. Some products use ingredients that naturally supply nitrate or nitrite, and those claims do not tell you how much sodium, saturated fat or total fat is in the food. The full label is more informative.

How to choose the better package for your goal

Compare calories, total fat and sodium at the same gram weight. Then look at saturated fat, protein and ingredients if they matter to your priorities. For lower calories and total fat, turkey bacon often comes out ahead. For lower sodium, either one can win, so the brand-specific panel is essential.

If you are trying to reduce processed meat overall, rotate bacon with less processed foods rather than relying solely on a turkey substitution. If you simply want the flavor of bacon in a sandwich or salad, a smaller amount of the version you enjoy may also work better than a larger amount chosen because the package sounds healthier.

The bottom line is nuanced but useful: turkey bacon is commonly leaner and lower in calories, while sodium has no guaranteed winner. Check equivalent portions before deciding which product better fits your diet.
